outcome: As of 11 Oct 2026 no accepted unconditional proof, counterexample or finiteness theorem for the integer problem was found in any source I could reach; in-window activity is a 2024 journal paper claiming a complete elementary proof that no expert engagement I could find has examined, an unrefereed June 2026 preprint whose non-existence step is conditional by its own account, a Lean-checked proof of 6 Oct 2026 that is conditional on explicit abc and a Dusart-type bound, a restricted-case theorem (Naciri, Integers 2025), and variant or generalised results that do not settle the classical equation.
problem_asks: (1) Whether any positive integer n outside {4, 5, 7} makes n!+1 a perfect square, i.e. whether the set of n with n!+1 = m² (m an integer) is exactly {4, 5, 7}. This splits into: (a) no n ≥ 8 is a solution; and the smaller n are already settled by direct check, namely n = 1, 2, 3, 6 give 2, 3, 7, 721, none a square (n = 0 gives 2, also not a square). (2) Equivalently, whether the three known pairs (n,m) = (4,5), (5,11), (7,71) are the complete list of pairs, since m is determined as the positive square root once n is fixed. The bullet does not ask for finiteness of the solution set as such, nor for any bound on n; a finiteness theorem would not by itself answer whether 4, 5, 7 are the only solutions.

events.what_happened: Salvador Cerdá, 'The Brocard-Ramanujan's Diophantine Equation n!+1=m²', arXiv 1504.06694. Abstract (verbatim, v4 page): 'In this paper we present a method to find the solutions to the Brocard-Ramanujan's problem n!+1=m^2.' The page now states the paper is withdrawn by the author. The comments field says an earlier version was withdrawn 'due to a logical fallacy detected by a reviewer', that the newer version 'was solved using modular congruence techniques', and 'There is a mistake at the solution'. The page does not state that no other solutions exist. An earlier search summary described this paper as reporting no further solutions; the fetched abstract and comments do not support that reading.
events.revisions: v1 25 Apr 2015; v2 28 Apr 2015; v3 30 Apr 2015 (withdrawn); v4 18 Feb 2016; v5 2 Mar 2016 (withdrawn).
events.delivers: Nothing established: the version carrying the method is withdrawn, and the author's own comment records an error in the solution.
events.remains: All of problem_asks.
events.doubts: Withdrawn by the author; the withdrawn-version comment cites a reviewer's logical-fallacy objection; the v4 comment itself says 'There is a mistake at the solution'.

withdrawn.what: Withdrawn by the author in v3 (30 Apr 2015) and v5 (2 Mar 2016); the comments give a reviewer's objection of a logical fallacy and say the solution contains a mistake.

The paper does not claim to resolve n!+1=m²; it describes semi-algorithms that halt iff a hypothesis fails.

events.what_happened: Theophilus Agama, 'The diagonalization method and Brocard's problem', arXiv 1803.09155 (single author). Applies a diagonalization method to equations Γ_r(n)+k = m², where Γ_r(n) = n(n-1)...(n-r) is a truncated product; for fixed k and r it claims finitely many solutions n > r. The classical equation corresponds to a truncation length growing with n, which the abstract does not treat.
events.delivers: Finiteness for each fixed pair (r, k): a finite analogue of the problem, not the classical equation.
events.remains: The classical n!+1=m² (truncation length tied to n), i.e. all of problem_asks.
events.direction: Analogue (fixed truncation); cuts toward finiteness only for the analogue.

events.what_happened: Somnath Maiti, 'Results of Brocard-Ramanujan problem on diophantine equation n!+1=m²', arXiv 2004.09256 (single author; no journal reference). The v1 abstract (read via the arXiv abstract page) says the paper 'gives necessary and/or sufficient conditions' for solutions, and states verbatim 'it has only finitely many solutions which is not based on any conjecture', and that 'Nobody has discovered any new solution of the problem beyond n=4, 5 and 7'. It cites the Berndt-Galway search to 10^9. Criterion: for √(n!) = k + ε with 0 < ε < 1, a solution exists iff n! = k(k+2) with ε and k strictly increasing.
events.revisions: v1 9 Apr 2020 (13 pages per comments field); v2 5 Feb 2026 (19 KB). I could not identify what changed in v2; the v2 abstract retains the finiteness claim.
events.delivers: Claimed unconditional finiteness of the solution set; no identification of the solutions. The criterion is a reformulation of the equation.
events.remains: Whether the solutions are exactly {4, 5, 7} (the bullet's question); the finiteness claim itself is unverified in any source I found.
events.time_since_posted: about 6.5 years since v1; v2 (Feb 2026) with no engagement found
events.doubts: Unconditional finiteness is claimed here, while Overholt (1993), Dąbrowski (1996), Luca (2002) and Naciri (2025) give only conditional or restricted finiteness, and the Erdős problem page and the 2026 literature still describe finiteness as conditional or restricted. No journal publication and no reviewer found. The Maiti abstract's 'no new solution' statement is a report of search results, not a proof. A secondary summary also reports a heuristic 'almost impossibility' argument; I did not verify it from the full text.
events.direction: Asserts unconditional finiteness, which would make the question a finite check; it does not itself say whether 4, 5, 7 are all the solutions.

The Springer page redirected to a login page and I did not read the paper; the content is taken from the Maiti abstract (which states the 2000 search) and from the Wikipedia article.

events.remains: All of problem_asks (the universal claim for n > 10^9).

events.what_happened: Abderrahim Makki Naciri, 'On the Brocard-Ramanujan equation with 7-free integers and prime powers', Integers 25 (2025), #A71, published 15 Aug 2025 (received Jan 2025), per a search summary. The result: for every integer k ≥ 2, finitely many integer solutions (n,x) of n!+1=x² assuming x±1 is k-free or has fewer than k prime divisors; when x±1 is 7-free (or a prime power) all solutions are identified, and they are n = 4, 5, 7. The Colgate PDF returned a binary/unreadable response to my fetcher; these details come from a search summary and from the Erdős problem #398 page (opened), which lists the same result as [Na25].
events.revisions: No arXiv or other preprint found; the date given is the journal publication, the first public version I could find.
events.delivers: Within the restricted class where x±1 is 7-free (or a prime power), only n = 4, 5, 7. Finiteness of solutions under k-free hypotheses for every k ≥ 2.
events.remains: The unrestricted problem: x±1 without the k-free or prime-power hypothesis, where neither finiteness nor the identification is given.

events.direction: Restricted case: in the 7-free (prime-power) class, n = 4, 5, 7 are the only solutions, which cuts toward the conjectured answer for that class; the general case is not addressed.

events.what_happened: Arvind Naladiga Venkat, 'Perfect Squares from Sums of Consecutive Factorials: Discovery of an Exceptional Solution to a Generalized Brocard-Ramanujan Problem'. Equation Σ_{i=0}^{a} (n+i)! + 1 = k². Reports (n,k,a) = (4,215,4): 4!+5!+6!+7!+8!+1 = 46,225 = 215². A computer search over n ≤ 30,000 and a ≤ 100 found seven solutions, and the author conjectures these are all positive solutions. The a = 0 case is the classical equation. Read only through a third-party aggregator (synapsesocial), which gives a posting date of 17 Jan 2026 while the citation reads 2025 and the PDF is named venkat-2025_v2; the arXiv record was not found.
events.revisions: Possibly v2 (per the PDF filename); not verified.
events.delivers: For the generalised sum equation with a ≥ 1: a computer search and a conjecture; no new solution for a = 0.
events.remains: The classical equation (a = 0): nothing established. The generalised equation: complete classification, as conjectured.
events.directly_checkable: The new solution can be checked by hand: 4!+5!+6!+7!+8!+1 = 46,225 = 215².
events.doubts: The posting date conflicts between the aggregator (17 Jan 2026) and the citation/filename (2025); the PDF was not read.
events.direction: Neighbouring generalisation; the new solution is for a = 4 and does not bear on a = 0.
events.object: Solution (n,k,a) = (4,215,4) of the generalised sum equation: 4!+5!+6!+7!+8!+1 = 215². Explicit; checkable by arithmetic. It is not a solution of n!+1=m².

events.what_happened: Saša Novaković, 'The Diophantine equation P(x) = ∏ H_{n_i}', arXiv 2601.16757 (v1 only, 23 Jan 2026, 9 pages). Motivated by Naciri's result; proves analogous statements for P(x) = ∏_{i=1}^{r} H_{n_i}, where P is a polynomial and H_{n_i} are divisible sequences. Its abstract recalls that Naciri proved finiteness for n!+1=x² under an assumption on x±1; the abstract sentence 'the Brocard-Ramanujan equation n!+1=x² has only finitely many integer solutions' is that recollection of the conditional result, not a new unconditional claim.

events.remains: All of problem_asks.
events.direction: Analogue; no bearing on the classical equation beyond restating Naciri.

events.what_happened: Leandro Vieira Peixoto (no affiliation given), 'The Brocard Problem: Structural Invariants, p-Adic Density, and the Generative Sieve', arXiv 2606.23485 (v1 only, 22 Jun 2026; math.NT, cross-listed math.OC; 29 pages). Claims: a 'Triangular Equivalence' (a Brown number exists exactly when one-eighth of n! is a triangular number); Theorems 1-3 (for prime p > 7, (p#)² < p!; the modular integer b must be divisible by 4; the triangular equivalence); a 'generative p-Adic Sieve' and LLL-based approximation; recursive reductions for even shifts; and a rule-out of n!+3=m² for n ≥ 4 by a mod-4 argument. Section 2 states the conditional: 'If it can be rigorously demonstrated that k cannot be strictly greater than zero ... then Brocard's Conjecture is definitively proven.' Section 3.2.1 says 'k=0 has been proven to yield no solutions for n>8' (no source is identified in the text I read). Section 5.3 says the reformulation 'does not, by itself, rigorously prove their absolute non-existence'. Section 7.3 says a rigorous quantitative constraint 'remains an open problem'. The quotations come from a fetcher's extraction of the arXiv HTML; the PDF was not decodable.
events.delivers: (a) The triangular equivalence: n!+1 = m² with m = 2Y+1 holds iff n! = 4Y(Y+1), i.e. iff n!/8 is triangular; this is an elementary restatement, which I checked by hand, and says nothing about which n work. (b) The n!+3 mod-4 rule-out, correct but about a different equation. (c) The k = 0 case, which the paper says is proven for n > 8; the source is not identified in what I read. (d) The sieve and LLL claims, which the Pith review says lack code or derivation.
events.remains: The step excluding k > 0 (which the paper itself states as conditional); the rigorous non-existence for all n; therefore the full question of problem_asks.

checked_by.qualification: an AI model, not a human expert
checked_by.what_they_did: Read the paper on 26 Jun 2026 and answered fixed questions. Found the triangular equivalence and the +3 invalidation correct; found the sieve and LLL claims unsupported by explicit code or timing data; said the work 'does not resolve the main open question'; recommended peer review. The Pith page states 'No human expert has reviewed this paper yet'.

events.directly_checkable: The triangular equivalence is an elementary identity (n! = 4Y(Y+1) ⇔ n!+1 = (2Y+1)²) and can be checked by hand. The sieve and the k = 0 step are not given in a form I could check.
events.doubts: Single author with no affiliation; the paper's own §2 and §5.3 say the non-existence is conditional; §7 calls the sieve 'weak evidence'; the Pith review says the structural framing largely restates prime factors already present in n!; the 'k = 0 proven' claim in §3.2.1 has no cited source in the text I read; no human review.
events.direction: Cuts toward the conjectured answer only in conditional form: by its own §2 the exclusion of solutions reduces to showing k cannot be positive, and §5.3 disclaims an absolute non-existence proof.

events.what_happened: Eric F. Bravo, 'On Brocard's problem with Padovan and Perrin numbers', arXiv 2606.28577 (v1 only, 26 Jun 2026; math.NT; MSC 11B39, 11D88). Solves n!+1 = x² with x a Padovan number, and separately with x a Perrin number; in both cases (n,x) = (4,5) is the only solution. Per the Pith summary, the method is growth comparison plus modular checks for linear recurrences with bases below 2.
events.delivers: Restricted to x in the Padovan or Perrin sequences: (4,5) is the only solution in both. It says nothing about x in general.
events.remains: The classical problem with x arbitrary, i.e. all of problem_asks.

events.what_happened: Roman Lakovskiy (GitHub: LakovskyR), 'Brocard's equation under explicit abc: cutoff 1038, witness certificate and Lean proof', GitHub repository brocard-abc and Zenodo software deposit v1.1.0 (6 Oct 2026). README: a conditional proof that n!+1=m² has only n = 4, 5, 7. Main route: H1 is the explicit abc form of Laishram and Shorey with ε = 34/71 ('LS_abc_34_71'); H2 is ∏_{p≤n} p ≤ 2.7186^n (Dusart). A witness certificate with 1031 primes excludes 8 ≤ n ≤ 1038; the abc argument covers n ≥ 1039. The Lean 4 theorem Brocard.brocard_of_LS takes H1 and H2 as hypotheses. A remark via Zhou's 'Theorem A1(i)' says the certificate with that theorem gives the result without H2; the README says this route 'relies on inter-universal Teichmüller theory, whose correctness is disputed', and 'the preprint has not been refereed'. Browkin's hypothesis abc(1.8) (earlier) is cited as giving the same conclusion for n > 7 under that hypothesis.
events.revisions: Zenodo software record v1.1.0 (6 Oct 2026), a supplement to GitHub tag v1.1.0. Earlier releases and first commit dates are not shown on the pages I read; the GitHub repo lists 6 commits.
events.delivers: Conditional on H1 and H2: no n ≥ 8 gives a square; with n ≤ 7 settled by direct check, the solution set is {4, 5, 7}. Unconditionally: nothing.
events.remains: The unconditional problem. H1 and H2 are not proved in the record. The second route, which the author says avoids H2, relies on the IUT-based result that the author flags as disputed.

machine_checked.system: Lean 4 (toolchain leanprover/lean4:v4.33.1 and Mathlib v4.33.1, per README)

events.directly_checkable: The 1031-prime witness certificate and the Lean build can be rerun with the README's commands (lake build; reproduce.sh). I did not rebuild them. 'Sorry-free' is inferred from the README's list of axioms (propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound), not from a build I ran.
events.doubts: The result is conditional on explicit abc (unproven) and Dusart-type bound H2; the second route relies on IUT, which the README itself says is disputed and whose acceptance is unsettled in the wider literature. The Zhou 'Theorem A1' cited in the README could not be located in sources I could reach. Single author, no referee, no discussion found. Zenodo DOI mismatch: the GitHub badge gives 10.5281/zenodo.23175570, while the record I fetched is 10.5281/zenodo.23184349.
events.direction: Conditional: cuts toward the conjectured answer (no solutions beyond 4, 5, 7) under H1 and H2.
events.object: No counterexample. A finite certificate: 1031 witness primes that exclude each n from 8 to 1038 by a computation the README describes; explicit and computational, not a non-constructive argument.

events.what_happened: ProofAtlas 'Brocard's Problem' collaboration page (proofatlas.ai), described as 'AI-first mathematical research · exact proof evidence'. Problem stated as n!+1=m² ⇒ n ∈ {4,5,7}. Reports exact arithmetic reductions and finite certificates; a GMP scan through n = 10,000 is listed as 'reported unreproduced' ('Intake did not execute the program'); the universal step for n ≥ 8 is listed as open. The page says 'Status and source checked August 28, 2026; next context review due November 28, 2026'. It names no AI system, model or lab, and does not say who produced the packet.
events.delivers: Reductions and a finite scan, which the page itself says are not a proof; no completed resolution.
events.remains: All of problem_asks (the page lists the universal step as open).
events.doubts: The GMP scan is 'reported unreproduced' and the page says it 'is not proof for all n'. First public date not established.
events.direction: Claims no completed proof; the scan and reductions cut toward the conjectured answer only for the checked range.

disputes.summary: Maiti (arXiv 2004.09256, v1 2020; v2 Feb 2026) claims unconditional finiteness ('not based on any conjecture'). Overholt (1993), Dąbrowski (1996), Luca (2002), Naciri (2025) and the Erdős problem #398 page treat finiteness as conditional or restricted, and Wikipedia gives only the conditional results.

Several unrefereed complete-solution claims for the classical equation exist with no priority contest in the sources I read: Cerdá (2015, withdrawn), Sabihi (2017, critiqued Nov 2025), Sultan (2021, unread), Karimullah (IJAM, 30 Apr 2024), and the Lakovskiy conditional proof (6 Oct 2026). Only the Sabihi claim was examined in public, and only for specific errors.

Matson's search bound is disputed: the Erdős forum (18 Apr 2026) gives n ≤ 4·10^11; the OEIS A085692 comment (28 Oct 2019) gives n ≤ 10^12; the jhg023 README says 10^12 had been tested before 2020. The 10^15 search is attributed to Epstein and Glickman by the forum, which the repository does not confirm.

summary: No source I could reach contains an accepted unconditional proof, a counterexample, or a finiteness theorem that settles whether n!+1 is a square only for n = 4, 5, 7. The Erdős problem page for #398 (last edited 1 Apr 2026) shows no status label but still treats the question as open, and the Wikipedia lead (as read) still says it is not known whether there are more solutions. In-window activity, by date: (1) Karimullah, Indian Journal of Advanced Mathematics, published 30 Apr 2024, claims a complete elementary proof (n! = 4AB and an inequality for even n); the odd-n case is asserted by analogy and not shown in the abstract, and no expert engagement turned up in the Erdős forum or elsewhere; the journal's peer-review process is not documented on the page I read, so whether it counts as checked is a close call. (2) Naciri, Integers 25 (2025), #A71: a restricted-case theorem, finiteness under k-free hypotheses on x±1 and, when x±1 is 7-free (or a prime power), the identification n ∈ {4, 5, 7}; the forum confirms only the easy parts; I could not read the article PDF. (3) Takeda, Finite Fields and Their Applications (online 30 Sep 2025), a complete solution of the polynomial analogue over finite fields, which the institution's press release says is not the integer problem. (4) Peixoto, arXiv 2606.23485 (22 Jun 2026), a single-author preprint with no affiliation: its 'triangular equivalence' is an elementary restatement which I checked by hand; its non-existence step is conditional by its own §2 and §5.3; its only review is an automated AI referee (grok-4.3, via Pith), which says no human has reviewed it. (5) Lakovskiy, GitHub/Zenodo, 6 Oct 2026: a Lean 4 proof conditional on an explicit abc hypothesis (Laishram-Shorey, ε = 34/71) and a Dusart-type bound H2, with a 1031-prime certificate covering 8 ≤ n ≤ 1038; the author's second route depends on inter-universal Teichmüller theory, which the author himself flags as disputed. (6) Variant and generalised work that does not settle the classical equation: Novaković (23 Jan 2026 and 10 Feb 2026), Bravo (26 Jun 2026, Padovan/Perrin: (4,5) only), Venkat (17 Jan 2026 per an aggregator; the citation says 2025; a generalised sum equation with the new solution (4,215,4)). (7) Two in-window events that are not new results: Maiti's 2020 finiteness claim gained an unexplained v2 in Feb 2026, and the DeepMind formal-conjectures issue #1417 (27 Dec 2025, closed) is a formal statement only. Pre-window events include Berndt-Galway (2000, n ≤ 10^9), Peters (2006, n ≤ 4·10^9), a 10^15 search (repository, 2020), the Overholt/Dąbrowski/Luca conditional finiteness results (1993-2002), the Sabihi preprint (ResearchGate, Jan 2017; its errors were pointed out in the Erdős forum in Nov 2025), and the Cerdá preprint (withdrawn 2015/2016). AI involvement: no source I read credits an AI system with the mathematics of the integer problem. The AI-related items are (a) automated AI referee reports on Peixoto and Bravo (grok-4.3, via Pith), which review the work and do not contribute to it; (b) a ChatGPT 'quick opinion' link in the Erdős forum thread (Nov 2025, comment by StijnC) that appears to be an AI check of the Sabihi paper; I did not open it, and it is a checking role, so none_found is false and systems is empty; (c) the ProofAtlas page, which calls itself 'AI-first' and offers a hosted agent but names no system and does not say who produced its packet, so none_found is null. OpenAI's Astra release (1 Aug 2026; ten Lean-certified results) was checked directly: the openai/ten-proofs README and file list contain none of the terms 'Brocard', 'Brown numbers', 'n!+1', 'factorial' or 'square', and none of the ten named results is this problem. Close calls: (a) whether the Karimullah 2024 claim counts as a resolution, given the journal acceptance and the unshown odd case; (b) whether the Lakovskiy proof counts, given that its hypotheses are unproven and its second route depends on contested IUT; (c) whether Maiti's 2020 'unconditional' finiteness claim is credible, given that the rest of the literature treats finiteness as conditional. Both readings are recorded in the events rather than resolved here.
competing_reading: The Karimullah paper (accepted and published by a journal in April 2024) and the Lakovskiy argument (Lean-checked, 6 Oct 2026) could be read as settling the problem: a journal accepted a complete proof, and a machine checks the other. Against that: the Karimullah odd case is not shown, no expert has engaged with the paper in the places I searched, the Lean proof rests on two unproven hypotheses, and the second route depends on IUT, which its own author flags as disputed. Peixoto's §2 could also be read as a complete reduction to the single claim that k cannot be positive, but the paper states that step is not proved, and its §3.2.1 claim that k = 0 is 'proven' has no identified source.
what_would_settle_it: For Karimullah: a number theorist's check of the even-n inequality (x < 2y and the x ≥ 3 contradiction) and a worked odd-n case, from the IJAM text; a published reply or correction. For Lakovskiy: a proof of H1 (explicit abc with ε = 34/71) or of H2, or an unconditional route, and an IUT specialist's check of the second route. For Peixoto: the source of the 'k = 0 has been proven' statement in §3.2.1, and a proof of the step §2 says is needed. For Maiti: the v2 changes and a referee report on the claimed unconditional finiteness. For Naciri: the article text (Integers 25, A71) to confirm the hypotheses and the classification. For the whole question: a refereed proof, a refereed counterexample, or a Lean formalisation of an unconditional statement.

incomplete: (1) Sabihi (2017): the ResearchGate text was not readable (HTTP 403). The claim is described from a search summary and the Erdős forum, and I did not verify the method or the abstract. (2) Naciri (2025): the Integers PDF was not readable; the hypotheses and classification come from the Erdős page and a search summary, and the 15 Aug 2025 date is the journal's publication date from the same summary. (3) Karimullah (2024): I read the IJAM landing-page abstract and the Zenodo description, not the full PDF; the even-n inequality and the odd-n case are unchecked. (4) Peixoto (2026): quotations come from a fetcher's extraction of the arXiv HTML and not from my own reading of the text. The PDF was not decodable. The §3.2.1 claim 'k = 0 has been proven' has no identified source. (5) Lakovskiy (2026): the Zenodo DOI in the badge (10.5281/zenodo.23175570) differs from the one the fetched record reports (10.5281/zenodo.23184349); no first-release date or earlier version was found; the Lean build was not rerun; 'sorry-free' is inferred from the README's axiom list; Zhou's 'Theorem A1' was not found. (6) Takeda (2025): the FFA paper was not read; the scope comes from the title and the press release; the Medium post returned HTTP 403. (7) ProofAtlas: no first public date. (8) Venkat: the arXiv record was not found and the PDF was not read; the date conflicts (2025 versus 17 Jan 2026). (9) Maiti (2020/2026): the v2 changes are unidentified and the full text was not read. (10) The pre-window primary sources for Overholt (1993), Dąbrowski (1996), Luca (2002), Gérardin (1906), Gupta (1935), Matson (2017), Berndt-Galway (2000) and Bolvardizadeh (2022/23) were not opened; their entries use secondary descriptions and say so. Matson's bound is disputed in the sources (4·10^11 versus 10^12). (11) The preprints.org manuscript 202303.0420 (HTTP 403) may have in-window versions, and I could not identify it. (12) The vixra Sultan claim was not read. (13) The Epstein-Glickman attribution of the 10^15 search is not confirmed by the repository. (14) No Google Scholar or MathSciNet access; the Erdős forum and Wikipedia were the main status sources, and they are secondary.
